answer: The sheather nails copper sheets to the hull below the waterline and counts every nail, sealing the count beside the ship's name. A yarrow sheet claimed as nailed fails the count: the nails must sit flush at the echo of the copper, and a sheet never nailed peels off in the first harbour. Buying a false sheathing record costs 18,200 in bribes to the sheather and fees to the yard, and the ocean count is checked at every careening, so a hull whose copper was never nailed fouls within a season.
